title: Everything that has breath
hook: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord (Psalm 150)
tomorrow: Zoe's boss wants her good deed on the company page. post it?

segments.voice: Yesterday: manifold works, goats on the hills, lions at night, a leviathan at play. Today the last psalm asks every one of them to join in.

Stadium crowds, church choirs, a song on somebody's late-night playlist: the word hallelujah gets around. And it's yesterday's answer. The last line of the last psalm, in the King James Bible, is "Praise ye the LORD," and in Hebrew that's one word: hallelujah, praise Yah. The whole book of Psalms ends on it. But Psalm 150 doesn't get there quietly. It gets there by making noise.
screen: `A WORD THAT GETS AROUND.` → `PRAISE YE THE LORD.` → `THE PSALMS END LOUD.`

segments.voice: Listen to the band this psalm calls in. "Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp. Praise him with the timbrel and dance." Then strings and pipes, then cymbals, the loud ones and the high sounding ones. Every instrument in the room. And then the last thing it calls on isn't an instrument at all: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." The trumpet needs breath. So does every living thing. The Bible also tells a story with that kind of noise in it. When the ark of God came up into Jerusalem, Second Samuel says "David danced before the LORD with all his might." His wife Michal watched from a window and despised him for it, a king leaping in the street. David's answer was that he'd make himself even lower than that, before the LORD. Psalm 150 calls for dance too, and some readers hear David's kind of praise in it: the whole body, unembarrassed. Here's one to tell a friend. The Hebrew word for breath in that last line is neshamah, and an old midrash plays on it: praise God for every single breath. That's the teaching in the psalm's last line, as Jews and Christians pray it: praise isn't only for the trained voice. Breath itself is enough to join. In Jewish morning prayer, Psalm 150 is among the psalms said before the main prayers.
screen: `TRUMPET, HARP, TIMBREL, CYMBALS.` · `THEN: EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.` · `DAVID DANCED WITH ALL HIS MIGHT.` · `NESHAMAH: EVERY SINGLE BREATH.` · then, large: `EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.`

segments.voice: Breathe in through your nose, and on each slow breath out, name one thing you're grateful for, silently or in a whisper. Count them on your fingers as they come, five, then ten if they keep coming. Let the last few breaths out be just breath.
Everything that has breath: the last call of the last psalm, after the trumpets and the cymbals, to anything alive.
For the road: every thing that hath breath, and that includes the breath you just took. The Psalms close on a hallelujah.

fork.setup: at a funeral, a cousin who never sings is too embarrassed to join the closing hymn. what does Psalm 150's last line offer her?
options: every thing that hath breath can praise; she doesn't need a trained voice.
she should just listen; the psalm gives praise to the trumpets and harps.

fork.reveal: the psalm runs through every instrument and then hands praise to anything that breathes. breath is enough to join.

chat.says: ray hums the last psalm while he cooks. says the whole book of psalms ends on one word?
options: Hallelujah, praise God. The last psalm gives it to everything with breath, not just the choir.
Amen. The book of Psalms ends by closing the prayer, the way a church service ends.
Peace. After all the trumpets and cymbals, the Psalms end in total silence.
chat.meaning: Psalm 150 ends "Praise ye the LORD," hallelujah in Hebrew, and after every instrument it calls on every thing that hath breath.
